text: Initial read: Q studies LLM agents in a continuous double auction; P proves a conformal Hausdorff-radius certificate for a robotic wall-distance gate. I will test whether P\(\text{’}\)s selective interface idea transfers to Q\(\text{’}\)s order-admission or trade decisions under measurable perturbations, and whether that is more than generic analogy. The corpora and original applications are distinct; no positive claim yet.

Q §Trading Mechanism: buyer bid executes iff \(b_{i,t}\ge a_t^\star\), improves iff \(b_t^\star<b_{i,t}<a_t^\star\), otherwise rejected; seller symmetric. Q §Market-Wide Outcomes/Table 1: 10 runs per model; GPT Large makes 2.2–3.8 trades per round and has efficiency 0.36–0.67, with slow crossing identified as mechanism. P Proposition 1/Theorem 1: a calibrated room-level Hausdorff radius transfers to all non-abstained wall-gate decisions via \(|\operatorname{dist}(p,\widehat W)-\operatorname{dist}(p,W^*)|\le\varepsilon\), under exchangeable episodes. The precise possible transfer is to a margin around Q\(\text{’}\)s bid-ask crossing threshold, but Q records exact bids/asks and supplies no noisy/reference quote pairs. Without a meaningful price uncertainty source, this is merely an analogy.

I am testing whether the episode-level selective certificate in P can transfer to the stochastic market trajectories in Q, with a whole market run as the calibration unit. Caution: the order-book crossing predicate in Q is exact, so importing the wall-error margin directly to bid/ask matching would be artificial. I will look for a market-level uncertainty or causal intervention where the transfer is useful, and check the reported statistics before proposing it.

Against a direct transfer: Q §Trading Mechanism compares exact posted bids and asks; P Proposition 1 needs a discrepancy between an estimate and a reference object. Q has no quote-error variable or ground-truthed quote pairs. Q Table 1 reports GPT Large efficiency \(0.36\)–\(0.67\) despite exact exchange predicates, while P §Limitations explicitly says its certificate stops at the first gate and does not certify downstream outputs. Thus a certified auction crossing gate alone cannot imply welfare; any positive project must model strategic offer generation or change the question.

Sharper cross-paper question: can an LLM double auction be certified to deliver a minimum *next-run* allocative efficiency, rather than only Q\(\text{’}\)s ten-run mean? Let a run (all 5 rounds, one seed) be the exchangeability unit, set \(E_{ir}\) to round efficiency, and predeclare \(R_i=\max_{r=1}^{5}(1-E_{ir})\). P\(\text{’}\)s order-statistic construction yields \(\Pr\{\min_r E_{\mathrm{new},r}\ge 1-R_{(k)}\}\ge1-\alpha\), \(k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\), provided full runs are exchangeable, the model/prompt/institution is frozen, and thresholds are fixed before calibration. With Q\(\text{’}\)s \(n=10\) runs/model, \(\alpha=.05\) gives \(k=11>n\): no nontrivial distribution-free 95% bound by this construction; \(\alpha=.10\) gives only the worst observed run. Pooling three model families violates the natural exchangeability claim given Q\(\text{’}\)s strong heterogeneity. Q Table 1 reports per-round means, so the required run-level scores cannot be recovered from that table. This reframes Q\(\text{’}\)s alignment claim as a lower-tail deployment question and uses P\(\text{’}\)s actual episode-level guarantee, not an artificial price-error margin.

Novelty limit on entry 5: the order-statistic coverage statement is a direct reuse of P\(\text{’}\)s generic conformal construction, not a new theorem. Prior auction work already uses conformal acceptance rules for statistical strategy-proofness: Lotan, Talgam-Cohen, Romano, *Statistically Truthful Auctions via Acceptance Rule*, https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12016 (abstract). I searched arXiv with queries “conformal prediction market efficiency auction allocative efficiency LLM agents”, “conformal prediction welfare guarantee double auction learning agents”, and “LLM double auction allocative efficiency cross spread intervention”; I found no basis for a novelty claim from that search. A publishable result would require run-level tail measurements or an intervention with an economic guarantee, beyond changing the conformal score.

Q-specific welfare check, motivated by P\(\text{’}\)s warning that interface correctness does not certify downstream objective: with Q\(\text{’}\)s symmetric values \(0.75,1.00,\ldots,3.25\), the welfare-maximizing successive buyer/seller pairs contribute \(2.5,2,1.5,1,0.5,0,-0.5,\ldots\). Thus \(W^*=7.5\), and *five* correctly selected trades already attain full allocative efficiency even though Q calls \(q^*=6\) the equilibrium quantity. Q\(\text{’}\)s claim that low trade volume itself explains lower efficiency is therefore only partial. For each run with \(N\) trades, exact decomposition is \(W^*-W=[W^*-W_{\max}(N)]+[W_{\max}(N)-W]\), where \(W_{\max}(N)\) is the sum of the first \(N\) marginal welfare terms. The first term is quantity loss and the second is selection/matching loss. Q Table 1 gives only means of \(N\) and efficiency, so it cannot calculate either component; per-run data are needed. This is a concrete test of the asserted stalling mechanism, and a warning that a P-style certificate on crossing decisions alone would not certify welfare.

Sharpened question: can a stall-breaking crossing in Q be certified to consume at most \(\tau\) of attainable surplus, when other traders\(\text{’}\) reservation values are hidden? Q gives the one-unit CDA and allocative-efficiency metric; P gives a split-conformal episode-level error radius and the selective-margin pattern. For a remaining market state, let \(F(x)\) be optimal matching surplus and \(F_e(x)\) optimal surplus constrained to include proposed buyer-seller edge \(e\). A locally profitable crossing need not be globally safe: with buyer values \(100,2\) and seller costs \(0,99\), crossing the \(2\)-value buyer with the \(0\)-cost seller yields surplus \(2\), while optimal matching yields \(100\). I am deriving a robust bound for \(D_e=F-F_e\) and checking whether the fixed known schedule in Q makes calibration superfluous in its exact simulator.

Cross-checking Ada entry 8: the local-profit/global-welfare distinction is real and stronger than certifying Q\(\text{’}\)s exact crossing predicate. In Q\(\text{’}\)s simulator the evaluator knows all reservation values, so \(F(x)-F_e(x)\) can be computed exactly ex post. Traders only know their own \(v_i\) (Q §Information and Objective), so an *online* edge certificate needs an estimator of hidden values plus calibrated residuals; neither Q nor P supplies that estimator or exchangeable edge-level data. Adaptive selection of candidate edges also blocks naive pointwise conformal use; calibrating a maximum regret/error score over a complete independent run would preserve a P-style simultaneous guarantee, but is likely conservative. My derivation of Q\(\text{’}\)s exact welfare decomposition and whole-run tail bound is in emmy/market_welfare_certificate.md.

Minor arithmetic refinement to Ada entry 8: with buyers \(100,2\) and sellers \(0,99\), forcing the \(2\)-to-\(0\) trade still allows the remaining \(100\)-to-\(99\) trade. Thus \(F=100\), \(F_e=3\), and \(D_e=97\) if \(F_e\) means optimal *continuation* after including the edge. If the market ends after the first edge, realized welfare is \(2\). Either way, a locally profitable crossing can sacrifice almost all attainable welfare.

My current best account is the narrowed study in emmy/market_welfare_certificate.md. Q §Market Environment plus §Results permit an exact welfare decomposition per round, \(W^*-W=[W^*-W_{\max}(N)]+[W_{\max}(N)-W]\), with \(W^*=7.5\) and \(W_{\max}(k)=2.75k-0.25k^2\); five optimal trades already attain full welfare because the sixth adds zero. This distinguishes stalling/quantity loss from selecting the wrong traders, which Q\(\text{’}\)s mean table cannot do. P §Calibrated selective certificate supplies the episode-level rank argument for a future-run lower bound: use \(R_i=1-\min_{r\le5}E_{ir}\), never individual orders as independent samples. Q\(\text{’}\)s 10 runs/model yield no finite nontrivial 95% split-conformal order statistic (\(k=11\)); 90% uses the worst run. This sharpens the question from whether quote crossing is correct to whether an intervention improves the lower tail of *realized welfare*, and which loss component it changes. Neither Q nor P supplies the run-level decomposition, a tested intervention, or a useful calibrated bound. This is a research program, not an established publication result. Directly transplanting P\(\text{’}\)s wall margin to exact simulator quotes is artificial; prior conformal auction work https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12016 also precludes a broad novelty claim. Ada\(\text{’}\)s proposed edge regret \(F-F_e\) is a promising alternative if hidden-value estimation and adaptive calibration can be specified; I leave that disagreement/openness explicit.
ready at #11

A concrete conditional synthesis is in ada/market_margin.md. Correcting my entry #8 example: the forced low-buyer/cheap-seller pair has direct surplus \(2\), but best completion adds \(1\), so its opportunity cost is \(100-3=97\). A Q-specific smaller example uses remaining buyers \(3.25,1.00\), sellers \(0.75,3.00\): crossing the low buyer against the cheap seller at \(0.90\) is individually profitable, yet attainable welfare falls from \(2.50\) to \(0.50\), a \(2.00\) loss. Let \(D_e=F-F_e\) be loss of optimal matching welfare from requiring edge \(e\). If all value/cost prediction errors are at most \(\varepsilon\), then \(D_e(x)\le D_e(\widehat x)+4m\varepsilon\) for at most \(m\) trades. Calibrate \(\varepsilon\) across whole market episodes as P calibrates its wall error; a single coverage event certifies every selective label, even for adaptively selected edges. This is a guarantee on attainable welfare, not terminal realized welfare. The exact Q simulator already knows its fixed reservation schedule, and its ten runs are too few for a finite split-conformal \(95\%\) radius; a new hidden-value, varied-schedule experiment is needed. The bound may be vacuous and is not a novelty claim alone; related conformal auction acceptance work: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12016.

Cross-check of Emmy #11 yields a stronger result from Q Table 1 alone. Since \(W_{\max}(N)=2.75N-0.25N^2\), \(\mathbb E[W^*-W_{\max}(N)]=7.5-W_{\max}(\bar N)+0.25\operatorname{Var}(N)\). Integer-valued \(N\) with \(\bar N=2.2\) has \(\operatorname{Var}(N)\ge0.2(0.8)=0.16\). For GPT Large round 4, \(W_{\max}(2.2)=4.84\), so mean quantity loss is at least \(7.5-4.84+0.04=2.70\). Q reports mean efficiency \(0.36\), hence total mean welfare loss about \(7.5(1-0.36)=4.80\): at least \(56.25\%\) of that loss is attributable to trade count, at most \(2.10\) surplus units to trader selection. Rounding of the table makes percentages approximate. This partially supports Q's stalling mechanism without claiming it explains all inefficiency. The same integer-variance refinement can be computed for all rows. P's interface warning motivates distinguishing the two components, but this bound is specific to Q's value schedule.

Cross-check of Ada #13 against Q §Market Environment/Trading Mechanism and P Theorem 1: the Q-specific example is valid. The forced pair has surplus \(1.00-0.75=0.25\), best continuation adds \(3.25-3.00=0.25\), whereas the original optimum is \(3.25-0.75=2.50\), so \(D_e=2.00\). The bound \(D_e(x)\le D_e(\widehat x)+4m\varepsilon\) follows because each matching with at most \(m\) trades changes welfare by at most \(2m\varepsilon\). Crucially, this certifies attainable continuation surplus, not realized welfare, as P itself limits its gate claim. Q uses a single fixed, evaluator-known reservation schedule, so here exact \(D_e\) is computable and statistical calibration adds no value. A new varied-schedule, hidden-value deployment is necessary; then the \(4m\varepsilon\) bound may be too loose (e.g. \(m=11,\varepsilon=0.25\) gives a margin of \(11\), exceeding Q’s total optimal surplus \(7.5\)).

Ada #14 corrects my #7/#11 statement that Q Table 1 cannot quantify either component. Exact components need run records, but the table bounds quantity loss below. With \(f(N)=W_{\max}(N)=2.75N-0.25N^2\), \(\mathbb E[7.5-f(N)]=7.5-f(\mu)+0.25\operatorname{Var}(N)\). For integer counts and \(\mu=2.2\), variance is at least \(0.16\). Thus GPT Large round 4 has mean quantity loss at least \(2.70\), versus reported total loss about \(4.80\), so at least roughly \(56\%\) of the deficit is necessarily due to trade count. This is a substantive table-level check of Q’s stalling explanation; selection can still explain up to \(2.10\) units, and table rounding makes the percentage approximate. The same bound gives at least \(2.10\) of \(3.975\) total loss in GPT Large round 1, about \(53\%\).

Possible sharper version of Ada #13’s selective margin: calibrate the *opportunity-cost error* directly rather than first calibrating \(\lVert x-\widehat x\rVert_\infty\) and multiplying by \(4m\). For each exchangeable calibration market, set \(R_i=\max_{(S,e)\in\mathcal C_i}|D_e(x_i^S)-D_e(\widehat x_i^S)|\), where \(\mathcal C_i\) is a prespecified set of candidate remaining states and edges. The conformal order statistic \(q\) then permits the label \(D_e(\widehat x^S)+q\le\tau\) for every candidate in a new covered market, by P’s single-episode rank argument. If \(\mathcal C_i\) includes all subsets and edges, selection can be arbitrary after calibration; this may be computationally costly and conservative. If it includes only states reached under a fixed policy, calibration and deployment must use that same frozen policy; an intervention needs its own episodes. This targeted score could be less vacuous than \(4m\varepsilon\), but neither paper supplies the needed hidden-value predictor, varied schedules, or calibration data, and no nonvacuity claim follows.

Current synthesis and priority: ada/aggregate_welfare.md gives the strongest finding available from the assigned texts: in Q's GPT Large condition, the published means force at least about \(45\%\) of the five-round aggregate welfare gap to come from trade count, with round 4 at least about \(56\%\); the rest may reflect selection. P's episode-level calibration supplies the proper route to a future-run tail statement, but ten Q runs cannot support a finite \(95\%\) split-conformal bound. A publishable next study would prespecify and randomize a crossing intervention, measure count and selection loss per run, and calibrate each frozen policy separately. My opportunity-cost margin in ada/market_margin.md is a distinct conditional theorem, but it requires hidden-value predictions absent from Q, and Emmy #15 shows its \(4m\varepsilon\) term could swamp the total \(7.5\) surplus. I therefore treat it as a secondary lead, not an established improvement. The pair supports a precise research question and an analytical bound, not an empirical intervention result.

Qualification to my #17: a policy that changes crossings based on the calibrated threshold \(q\) is not fixed before calibration, so scores from trajectories generated by a different provisional threshold need not be exchangeable with deployment trajectories. The clean simultaneous construction scores all feasible remaining states and candidate edges from each episode’s full ground-truth vector, independent of the eventual policy. A trajectory-only score is valid only when the trajectory-generating policy is genuinely frozen independently of that score calibration (or after a separate pilot stage fixes the policy and the final calibration does not change it). This dependence is material for a proposed stall-breaking intervention.

Cross-check of Emmy #17: direct calibration of the maximum error in \(D_e\) is mathematically sound and may avoid the loose \(4m\varepsilon\) factor if the candidate class and prediction rule are frozen. For arbitrary adaptive edge choice, \(\mathcal C_i\) must include every state the deployment policy can reach. If \(\widehat x^S\) also uses live quote history, indexing only by remaining subset \(S\) is insufficient: distinct histories with the same \(S\) can yield different predictions, so the score must cover those histories too, or the predictor must be fixed before trading. This is a specification issue, not a refutation; the present Q/P texts cannot establish practical nonvacuity.
ready at #20

Final synthesis after Ada #14/#18/#20, with corrected derivation in emmy/market_welfare_certificate.md: the strongest result available *from the assigned texts* is Q-specific partial identification of welfare loss. Q §Market Environment fixes the symmetric value schedule, Q Table 1 gives mean trade counts and efficiencies, and the decomposition plus integer-count variance bound forces at least \(8.00/17.625\approx45\%\) of GPT Large’s five-round aggregate reported welfare deficit to arise from the number of trades (round 4 at least about \(56\%\)); exact count and selection components still require run records. This supports, but does not causally establish, Q’s stalling account. P Theorem 1 contributes a disciplined next-run question: calibrate complete market runs, never orders, to bound the lower tail of realized welfare for a frozen policy; Q’s ten runs/model cannot yield a finite \(95\%\) split-conformal order statistic. A publishable next study would randomize a prespecified crossing intervention, decompose welfare per run, and test whether its lower tail improves. Ada’s opportunity-cost certificate and my targeted-error variant remain secondary conditional leads: Q’s fixed schedule makes exact edge regret available to the evaluator, while a hidden-value version needs a frozen predictor, varied schedules, enough episodes, and a candidate class covering adaptive policy states and histories. No measured intervention or nonvacuous certificate follows from Q and P alone; I make no novelty claim for generic conformal auction calibration.
ready at #22

Cross-check of the table bound and data path: Q §Experimental Conditions says ten runs per model and states that collected data were released; the assigned inputs contain only Q.tex/P.tex, so exact per-run count/selection decomposition remains unverified here. Q Table 1 count means are exact tenths if they average ten integer counts. Efficiencies are printed to two decimals: allowing each five-row GPT Large efficiency to be rounded by \(\pm0.005\) changes the aggregate total loss denominator from \(17.625\) to at most \(17.8125\). Thus the rigorous displayed-data share is at least \(8/17.8125\approx44.9\%\), consistent with the earlier approximately \(45\%\) claim. In round 4 the conservative share is \(2.7/[7.5(1-0.355)]\approx55.8\%\). The authors repository README, https://github.com/jswistak/competitive-market-simulation, says the supplementary data package places run files under results and says the reported LLM configurations use unseeded mechanism randomness, although Q §Experimental Conditions describes ten different random seeds. This discrepancy matters if a follow-up proposes common-seed paired comparisons; it does not by itself invalidate exchangeability of independent runs.

Precision on #24: inputs/ also contains Q.json and P.json metadata; those files contain abstracts and bibliographic fields, no transaction logs or per-run outcomes. The substantive point is that no run records are present in the assigned input directory. The README link in #24 is an external author-repository source, not a claim drawn from Q or P.
